title: Feedback Should Improve the Teacher, Not the Lesson er-not-the-lesson/
author: Paul Cline
summary: Paul Cline extends Dylan Wiliam's principle that feedback should improve the learner, not the work into the domain of instructional coaching, asking what it means for a coach's feedback to improve the teacher rather than just the single observed lesson. He illustrates the idea with a real coaching episode: observing a language teacher introducing vocabulary, he forms a hypothesis (drawing on Adam Boxer's hypothesis model of observation) that displaying too many words at once will cause cognitive overload, then tests it directly by asking students individually - and finds his prediction wrong. Rather than treating the falsified hypothesis as wasted effort, Cline uses it to interrogate what a coach should actually do next: whether the underlying theory was wrong, irrelevant to this specific moment, or simply not the highest-leverage issue to raise given everything else competing for the teacher's attention. He generalises this into a broader argument about actionable coaching: an action step must be achievable, high-impact, motivating to the coachee, and not too far from their existing mental model of teaching, and it should be co-constructed rather than delivered top-down so the coachee understands the reasoning behind it. He closes with a compact summary list distilling these ideas into rules for generating, testing, and selecting coaching action steps that transfer beyond the single lesson observed.
points: Cline extends Dylan Wiliam's "feedback should improve the learner, not the work" from student feedback into teacher coaching, arguing the same logic should govern which action steps a coach chooses to give.

His live example - predicting cognitive overload from too much vocabulary on screen, then testing it by quizzing students directly - shows a coach's hypothesis being falsified in real time, and he treats that as useful data rather than a wasted prediction.
Cline argues a disconfirmed hypothesis doesn't necessarily mean the underlying theory is wrong for that teacher - it might just not be the highest-leverage problem to address in that specific lesson.

He closes with an explicit checklist for choosing coaching action steps, emphasising co-construction with the coachee and transferability across multiple future lessons over one-off, lesson-specific fixes.
quotes: One argument I’ve found useful in this context is to point out that my suggestions for improvement might not really make much impact on this piece of work, but they could be important on future pieces of work. This, I think, exemplifies the well known Dylan Wiliam adage that feedback should improve the learner, not the work.

Having read Adam Boxer’s post on the hypothesis model of observation, I make a prediction that some of the students will struggle to later match up the pronunciation and/or translation of the word with the written version because there is too much information to process in one place
There are (and have been), of course, times when my hypothesis will be correct, and that cognitive overload has interfered with students’ learning.
In this instance, however, it turns out that my prediction was wrong.

A coach needs to determine an action step that is achievable for their coachee, that will have a significant impact on student learning, that the coachee is motivated to work towards, and that doesn’t represent too big a departure from the coachee’s existing mental model of teaching.
Action steps need to be co-constructed with a coachee to ensure they understand the underlying principles of the strategy being suggested
High leverage action steps will be those that allow transfer to multiple situations, to increase the adaptive expertise of the teacher
